pipeline.description: AI discourse in the UK Parliament and the US Congress, 2023 to 2025, coded for the institutional pillar each speech invokes.
pipeline.unit: One transcript document (a UK Hansard debate or a US Congressional Record item).

codebook.title: Institutional pillars in AI regulation discourse
codebook.theory: Scott, W. R. (2014). Institutions and Organizations (4th ed.). Regulative, normative and cultural-cognitive pillars.
codebook.unit: One spoken contribution in a parliamentary debate.

question.instructions: You are coding one spoken contribution from a parliamentary debate. Decide which institutional pillar the contribution primarily invokes when it discusses artificial intelligence. Code only what the speaker says about AI; ignore other topics in the contribution. If several pillars appear, choose the one the speaker relies on most to make their argument.

options.regulative: AI is governed through rules, laws, regulation, enforcement, sanctions, liability, compliance or oversight bodies. The speaker appeals to what is legally required, permitted or punishable.
options.normative: AI is governed through values, norms, ethics, duties or professional standards. The speaker appeals to what is right, fair, responsible or appropriate, or to obligations owed to others.
options.cultural_cognitive: AI is understood through shared beliefs, taken-for-granted assumptions, frames or comparisons with others. The speaker appeals to what is inevitable, normal, or what other countries and organisations are doing.
options.residual: The contribution is substantively about AI, but invokes none of the three pillars, for example a purely technical, economic or anecdotal account.
options.not_relevant: The contribution mentions AI only in passing, or is not about AI.
